main_damage_causes: Nigel is a film-invented character who accumulates screen time and functional roles (communications officer, combatant, casualty) across multiple films, normalising a non-book presence in scenes that belong to established characters.

The most structurally damaging use is Nigel's apparent death in the Battle of Hogwarts (Scene 5), which uses an invented figure to deliver an emotional beat that should belong to a book character (e.g. Colin Creevey), diluting the earned weight of the battle's casualties.

Nigel's operational DA role in Deathly Hallows (Scene 3) slightly filters Neville's resistance leadership through an invented intermediary, weakening the clarity of the established characters' agency at a climactic moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Scene 2 (OotP) – DA training, Harry instructs Nigel in Stunning
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not establish Nigel as a named character; the DA training scenes in the books feature established student characters (Neville, Ginny, Luna, etc.) as Harry's primary students and interaction partners.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Nigel is used as Harry's primary demonstration partner for Stunning ('Come on, then, Nigel. Give me your best shot') and receives personal praise ('Good. Not bad at all, Nigel. Well done'), inserting a minor invented character into a role that belonged to established book characters.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Nigel is a film-only invention given small but recurring screen time that displaces interaction moments from named book characters. In isolation this is a minor issue, but it slightly dilutes the texture of the DA scenes.

damaging_scenes.scene: Scene 1 (GoF) – Nigel delivers Ron's parcel and is dismissed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not include Nigel as a character; parcel and message delivery functions are handled by owls or existing named characters.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Nigel appears as a small errand-running character who delivers Ron's parcel and is curtly dismissed ('Not now, Nigel. Later. Go on'), establishing him as a recurring minor presence with no book equivalent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The insertion is brief and causes negligible damage on its own, but begins the pattern of Nigel occupying screen space as a non-book character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Scene 3 (DH) – Nigel operates the wizard wireless as a DA communications officer
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not establish Nigel in any meaningful role; the DA's underground resistance network at Hogwarts in Deathly Hallows is led by Neville, Ginny, and Luna, with no invented intermediary characters given functional roles.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Nigel is given an active operational function: he operates the wizard wireless and broadcasts the coded message ('River, DA calling. Do you read? We have a new weather report: Lightning has struck') on Neville's instruction, making him a named agent in the DA's resistance network.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most damaging use of Nigel across the corpus. Giving a film-invented minor character a defined operational role in the DA's resistance at a structurally important moment (Harry's return to Hogwarts in the final film) slightly displaces focus and agency from established characters. The moment belongs to Neville's leadership arc but is filtered through an invented figure, weakening the sense that it is the core book characters holding the resistance together.

damaging_scenes.scene: Scene 4 (DH) – Nigel assists in placing magical charges on the Wooden Bridge
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not include Nigel in any active defensive role during the Battle of Hogwarts; the defensive preparation of Hogwarts is carried out by established characters.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Nigel is listed alongside Cho Chang and Katie Bell as one of the students directed by Seamus to place magical charges on key pressure points of the bridge, giving him a named combatant role in the battle.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Placing a film-invented character in the same breath as established book characters (Cho, Katie Bell) during a key battle sequence continues to normalise Nigel as a peer of real characters, subtly diluting the earned weight of those characters' participation in the climax.

damaging_scenes.scene: Scene 5 (DH) – Nigel's body is carried out of the Entrance Hall by Oliver Wood
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not include Nigel dying or being injured; casualties in the Battle of Hogwarts are established characters (Fred Weasley, Lupin, Tonks, Colin Creevey, etc.) whose deaths carry earned emotional weight from years of characterisation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Nigel is carried as an apparently dead or gravely wounded 'smallish boy' by Oliver Wood through the Entrance Hall, with Neville reacting to his fate, effectively using a film-invented character to deliver an emotional beat about fallen DA members.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the highest-impact unfaithful moment for Nigel. The emotional register of the Battle of Hogwarts casualties depends entirely on the audience's attachment to those characters. Using Nigel — an invented figure with no book presence — to stand in for a fallen student displaces Colin Creevey or other established characters who serve this exact narrative function in the books. It also gives Neville a grief reaction beat tied to a non-book character, weakening the authenticity of that emotional moment. The damage is at the relationship/arc level because it affects how the audience experiences the cost of the battle.

damaging_scenes.scene: Scene 2 (OotP) – Harry instructs Nigel one-on-one during Patronus lesson
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Harry's individual coaching during DA sessions is directed at established characters (notably Neville, whose arc of growing confidence is a key book thread).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Harry gives individual attention and encouragement to Nigel ('I know') during the Patronus training sequence, inserting the invented character into a mentorship beat.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor displacement of a mentorship moment from Neville or another established character to an invented one. Low individual damage but part of a cumulative pattern.
